decks.domain: Basic vehicle operation, turns, following distance, speed and right-of-way

cards.front: Who has the right-of-way at an intersection already occupied by others?
cards.back: On every road, pedestrians, bicyclists and other traffic that are already inside an intersection have the right-of-way over a driver arriving at it.
cards.memory_hook: Yield to traffic in the intersection

cards.front: How must a driver approach an intersection marked with a yield sign?
cards.back: Nearing an intersection with a yield right-of-way sign, you must travel slowly enough to stop if necessary and enter only when the way is clear.

cards.front: Who goes first at a four way stop, and who yields when two arrive together?
cards.back: At a four way stop the first vehicle to arrive has the right-of-way, and when two vehicles arrive at about the same time from different directions the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right.

cards.front: At a four way stop, when does the yield to the right rule apply?
cards.back: At a four way stop the rule is first to arrive goes first, and only when arrivals are simultaneous does the driver on the left yield to the driver on the right.

cards.front: To whom must a left turning driver yield?
cards.back: A driver turning left must yield to all oncoming traffic, because any vehicle coming toward you, whether a motor vehicle or a bicyclist, has the right-of-way.
cards.memory_hook: Left turns yield to oncoming traffic

cards.front: Who yields when entering a road from a driveway, alley, parking lot or T intersection?
cards.back: A driver coming onto a road out of a driveway, an alley, a parking lot or the stem of a T intersection gives the right-of-way to every vehicle already traveling on that road.
cards.memory_hook: Entering from a driveway or alley

cards.front: What must a driver do before entering any intersection?
cards.back: Before entering any intersection you must search in all directions and make sure you have a clear path through it.

decks.module: Speed maximums and safe speed for conditions
decks.domain: Basic vehicle operation, turns, following distance, speed and right-of-way

cards.front: What are the maximum speeds on Vermont roads and on the interstate?
cards.back: The maximum speed for any vehicle on all Vermont roads is fifty miles per hour or as posted, and on a Vermont interstate the maximum is sixty-five miles per hour or as posted.

cards.front: Where does the fifty mile per hour maximum apply, and where does sixty-five apply?
cards.back: Fifty miles per hour is the maximum on ordinary Vermont roads, while sixty-five miles per hour applies only on the interstate, and both are capped by whatever lower limit is posted.

cards.front: When must a driver slow below the posted limit?
cards.back: The law requires a vehicle to be under control at all times and driven at a speed that is reasonable for the dangers present, so at intersections, on curves, in heavy traffic, through construction zones, in bad weather and near pedestrians or bicyclists you must slow to a speed safe for conditions.

cards.front: What does the handbook say about crashes and speed for conditions?
cards.back: Many crashes are caused by driving too fast for conditions, and the handbook warns that even ten miles per hour can sometimes be an unsafe speed.

decks.module: Signal timing and the four second following distance
decks.domain: Basic vehicle operation, turns, following distance, speed and right-of-way

cards.front: How far ahead must a turn signal be given, and how many seconds satisfies it?
cards.back: The law requires a turn signal to be given not less than one hundred feet before turning or changing lanes, and signaling three to five seconds ahead satisfies that requirement.

cards.front: How does the signal law in feet relate to the three to five second habit?
cards.back: The signal law is written as a distance of not less than one hundred feet, while the practical habit is counted as three to five seconds before the turn or lane change.

cards.front: What do brake lights tell drivers behind, and what must you do if your lights fail?
cards.back: Pressing the brakes warns drivers behind that you intend to slow or stop, and if the directional or brake lights fail you are required to give hand signals instead and have the lights repaired at once.

cards.front: What is a visual search pattern and what does it help a driver notice?
cards.back: A visual search pattern is an orderly, repeating way of looking for hazards in every direction, including pedestrians, bicyclists and other vulnerable users, so the driver notices changing conditions in and around the intended path.

cards.front: What following distance does the four second method give, and when is more needed?
cards.back: The four second method leaves enough room to stop quickly behind the vehicle ahead, and when the road is poor, visibility is poor or speeds are higher the gap should grow beyond four seconds.
cards.memory_hook: Four seconds and when to add

cards.front: How is the four second following distance measured against a checkpoint?
cards.back: To measure four second spacing, note when the rear of the vehicle ahead passes a checkpoint such as a sign, driveway, pole or parked vehicle, count seconds until your vehicle reaches it, and fewer than four seconds means you are following too closely and must drop back.

cards.front: What is an easy way to count seconds for following distance?
cards.back: An easy way to count seconds for following distance is to say one thousand one, one thousand two and so on.

decks.domain: Basic vehicle operation, turns, following distance, speed and right-of-way

cards.front: What steps does a driver take when approaching a left turn?
cards.back: Approaching a left turn, signal three to five seconds in advance, slow gradually while checking the rearview mirror to confirm the driver behind understood, make sure no bicyclist or vehicle behind is trying to pass on your left, and on a multilane road be in the left lane well ahead of the turn without moving suddenly from the right lane.

cards.front: How should the vehicle be positioned and the wheels held while waiting to turn left?
cards.back: At the left turn itself, wait until no vehicles are oncoming, position the vehicle within one foot of the centerline when safe, and keep the wheels straight until you actually turn so a rear end hit will not push you into oncoming traffic.

cards.front: How does the setup distance differ between a left turn and a right turn?
cards.back: A left turn sets up within one foot of the centerline, whereas a right turn sets up about three feet from the right edge of the road.

cards.front: Who has the right-of-way over a left turning driver?
cards.back: Any oncoming vehicle or bicyclist has the right-of-way over a left turning driver, and pedestrians crossing the street you are turning into must also be yielded to.

cards.front: How is a left turn completed once the road is clear?
cards.back: Once the road is clear, complete the left turn at a proper speed keeping to the right of the center line, then check the rearview mirror and center the vehicle in its lane.

cards.front: In what order does a driver search the intersection before a left turn, and where does the vehicle enter the new street?
cards.back: Before a left turn the driver searches the intersection to the right, the front and the left, and enters the new street just to the right of its center line.

cards.front: How do the intersection search orders differ between a left turn and a right turn?
cards.back: A left turn search runs right, front, left, while a right turn search runs left, front, right and then quickly left again.

cards.front: How does a driver set up and signal for a right turn?
cards.back: On the approach to a right turn keep the vehicle roughly three feet from the road's right edge, never swing out to the left first, and put the signal on three to five seconds ahead while slowing and checking the mirror.

cards.front: In what order does a driver search before a right turn, and to whom must the driver yield?
cards.back: Before a right turn the driver searches the intersection left, front, right and then quickly left again, stays alert for bicyclists or pedestrians on the right side, must yield to any of them, and keeps close to the right side of the lane while turning.

cards.front: Which lane do you turn into on a multilane street, and what rule follows?
cards.back: When turning into a street with more than one lane in your direction, turn into the nearest lane, and then follow the multilane rule of driving on the right unless passing or turning.

decks.domain: Basic vehicle operation, turns, following distance, speed and right-of-way

cards.front: What is the first thing that must happen for a vehicle to stop?
cards.back: Even with ideal road and vehicle conditions and a fully alert driver, stopping a vehicle takes a great distance, and a stop requires that you see and recognize the danger before anything else happens.

cards.front: After recognizing danger, what three steps must happen before the vehicle stops?
cards.back: After the driver recognizes danger, the brain must tell the foot to brake, the foot must move to the pedal and operate it, and the brakes must work correctly before the vehicle stops.

cards.front: What is reaction distance, and how long does the average driver take to apply the brakes?
cards.back: Reaction distance is the distance traveled from the moment you see danger until you step on the brake, the average driver needs about three quarters of a second to apply the brakes, and higher speed means more distance covered before braking begins.

cards.front: How do reaction distance and braking distance differ, and which grows on wet roads?
cards.back: Reaction distance is covered before the brakes are touched, while braking distance is covered after they are applied, and only braking distance grows on wet, icy or gravel roads.

cards.front: What is braking distance, and when does it grow much longer?
cards.back: Braking distance is the distance traveled from the moment the brakes are applied until the vehicle stops, and it becomes much longer on wet, icy or gravel roads.

cards.front: Why is the road especially slippery when rain first begins?
cards.back: When rain first begins, oil, rubber, dirt and water mix to make the road especially slippery, which increases braking distance.

cards.front: What does the handbook say about left turns and crashes?
cards.back: Many crashes happen while a vehicle is turning left, and most of them would be avoided if the driver made the turn properly.

decks.module: Readiness, hand position and where to practice
decks.domain: Basic vehicle operation, turns, following distance, speed and right-of-way

cards.front: Does passing the written test by itself issue a learner's permit?
cards.back: Passing the written test does not by itself issue a learner's permit; the permit is issued only after every other requirement is met and every required document is provided.
cards.memory_hook: Passing the test is not enough

cards.front: What does the handbook say causes most crashes, and how can any motorist drive safely?
cards.back: Most motor vehicle crashes are caused by the actions or errors of the driver, and any motorist can drive safely through care, courtesy and caution and by modeling proper behavior.

cards.front: Where should a new permit holder begin practicing, and why?
cards.back: A new permit holder should begin practicing in an empty parking lot or on lightly traveled roads to build basic car control before moving to busier roads as skills improve.

cards.front: What must a slow driver do when traffic piles up behind?
cards.back: When a slow driver has traffic piling up behind, the law requires that driver to move to the roadside once it is safe and let the vehicles behind go past.
cards.memory_hook: Pull over when traffic backs up

cards.front: Where should the hands sit on the steering wheel, and how should turns be steered?
cards.back: Hands belong on the steering wheel at the nine and three or the eight and four clock positions, with hand over hand steering used for turns, while practicing left and right turns, smooth braking and controlled starts and stops.

cards.front: What should a driver do before moving the vehicle?
cards.back: Driver readiness before moving means adjusting the seat, adjusting all mirrors, testing the foot and parking brakes, adjusting and fastening the safety belt, locking the doors and turning on the headlights.

recap_hooks.text: Yield to traffic in the intersection
